description:
We are a team of enthusiastic computer science students passionate about technology, innovation, and solving real-world challenges. Our interests include artificial intelligence, software engineering, space exploration, and emerging technologies.

Our team brings together skills in Python, JavaScript, React, backend development, API integration, algorithms, data processing, AI technologies, and UI/UX design. We enjoy collaborating and turning creative ideas into practical solutions.
summary:
Imagine being one of the first astronauts to walk on Mars. You have a few hours of oxygen, an unfamiliar landscape ahead of you, and a scientific mission to complete. Where should you go? Which places are worth exploring? And most importantly, will you have enough oxygen to return to your base?

We built MarsNav to help answer these questions.

MarsNav is an interactive Mars exploration and mission planning platform that brings together real data collected by several NASA missions. It helps astronauts explore the Martian surface in 2D and 3D, understand the terrain, discover places of scientific interest, compare routes, and plan journeys within their available oxygen budget.

With an AI assistant, astronauts can plan scientific missions using everyday language, while our navigation tools help them adjust their routes when unexpected obstacles are encountered.

Through MarsNav, we hope to turn decades of robotic exploration into something that helps future astronauts make the most of every step they take on Mars.
details:
What exactly does it do?

MarsNav helps astronauts understand the terrain, find scientific locations, and plan journeys that consider terrain difficulty, available oxygen, and the return to base. It combines scientific discovery, mapping, navigation, and AI-assisted mission planning in a single platform.

How does it work?

Astronauts select a region they want to explore, and MarsNav automatically retrieves and analyzes available NASA data. Based on their scientific objectives, it suggests promising locations and plans routes between them while considering the available oxygen time. Astronauts can also report obstacles and find alternative routes during a navigation simulation.

What are the benefits?

  • Better-informed exploration: Helps astronauts understand the terrain and avoid unnecessarily difficult routes.
  • Scientific discovery: Finds promising locations that may be worth investigating.
  • Better use of oxygen and time: Helps astronauts visit scientific sites while accounting for the return journey.
  • Flexible mission planning: Allows astronauts to adjust their journeys when unexpected obstacles are encountered.
  • Accessible NASA data: Turns complex scientific information into easy-to-understand maps and visualizations.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming Languages: Python, TypeScript, JavaScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, HTTPX.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Zustand.
  • Mapping and Visualization: Leaflet, Three.js.
  • Route Planning: A* pathfinding algorithm.
  • Artificial Intelligence: Google Gemma API.
  • Development and Collaboration: Git, GitHub, Claude Code.
  • Hosting: Render (backend) and Vercel (frontend)

Interactive Website

Our website brings together the tools astronauts need to explore a region, discover scientific sites, plan a journey, and adapt their mission.

We wanted astronauts to spend less time figuring out how to use the technology and more time exploring Mars.

Automated Region Analysis and Interactive Maps

Astronauts simply select the area they want to explore, and MarsNav automatically retrieves the available NASA data and analyzes the terrain.

The interactive map allows astronauts to explore surface imagery, elevation, steepness, and possible signs of hydrated minerals through different map layers. The 3D view makes hills, valleys, and elevation changes easier to understand.

MarsNav retrieves only the scientific data needed for the selected region and saves the analyzed information for future use.

Scientific Site Discovery

One of the main reasons humans will travel to Mars is to make new scientific discoveries. MarsNav helps astronauts find places worth investigating based on their mission objectives.

It currently supports seven scientific objectives:

  • Hydrated Minerals: Locations showing possible signs of minerals associated with water.
  • Flat Terrain: Relatively flat areas for scientific activities.
  • High Vantage Points: Elevated locations for observing the surrounding landscape.
  • Lowest Ground: Low-lying areas and depressions.
  • Steep Cliffs: Large areas of steep terrain.
  • Ridges: Long, narrow, raised areas.
  • Crater-like Formations: Large, bowl-shaped depressions.

Six objectives use NASA elevation data, while hydrated mineral candidates are found using CRISM spectral data.

Each suggested location includes measurements and an explanation of why it was selected, helping astronauts decide which places are worth investigating further.

Beyond these seven objectives, MarsNav also helps astronauts explore other scientific interests by analyzing the terrain using available NASA data.

We tested MarsNav in the area around Jezero crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover landed, and found several promising geological features.

Intelligent Route Planning

The shortest route is not always the best route on Mars. A shorter path might cross steep terrain, while a slightly longer path could offer an easier journey.

MarsNav provides three route options:

  • Shortest Route: Prioritizes reducing travel distance.
  • Safest Route: Prioritizes gentler terrain based on available data.
  • Balanced Route: Balances distance and terrain difficulty.

Astronauts can compare travel time, distance, and elevation changes before choosing the most suitable route for their mission.

Oxygen-Aware Scientific Mission Planning

Every minute matters when an astronaut is exploring Mars.

MarsNav helps astronauts decide which scientific locations they can visit within their available oxygen time.

The platform selects promising locations, plans the journey between them, includes the return to base, and keeps additional time in reserve.

Astronauts can also see how their available time is divided and why certain locations were not included.

Instead of simply showing astronauts where interesting places are, MarsNav helps them decide which places they have enough time to visit and return from.

AI Mission Assistant

We wanted mission planning to be as simple as having a conversation.

Astronauts can simply tell MarsNav what they want to explore.

For example:

“I have four hours of oxygen. Find hydrated mineral sites near the base and plan a journey that returns to base.”

MarsNav then plans the journey and shows it directly on the map.

Astronauts can also ask questions about scientific locations, surrounding terrain, and NASA data.

Navigation and Obstacle Replanning

If astronauts encounter an unexpected obstacle, they can report it directly on the map. MarsNav calculates an alternative route while keeping the original route visible for comparison.

Our navigation simulation displays travel directions, remaining distance, estimated oxygen time, and upcoming terrain steepness.

Radiation Exposure Estimation

Using published measurements collected by NASA's Curiosity rover, MarsNav estimates typical radiation exposure for the planned duration of a Marswalk.

This helps astronauts understand how much radiation they may be exposed to and take it into account when planning their mission.

MarsNav in Future Mars Missions

While developing MarsNav, we also considered how it could work on Mars itself.

AI Without Depending on Earth

A question sent to an AI server on Earth could take tens of minutes to receive a response. For an astronaut with limited oxygen, waiting that long is not practical.

Due to the limited computing power of our development devices, we currently use Google's Gemma through its API. For actual Mars missions, the same open-weight model could run directly on a rover or habitat computer, allowing astronauts to interact with MarsNav without relying on communication with Earth.

Offline Exploration

Before leaving Earth, astronauts and mission planners could analyze the regions they expect to explore.

MarsNav already retrieves and saves analyzed scientific data for future use. By also storing map imagery locally, astronauts could explore these regions, plan scientific missions, and adjust their journeys without an internet connection.

Combined with the locally running Gemma model, this would allow MarsNav to operate independently of Earth.

Spacesuit Integration

Our prototype uses manually entered oxygen time. In actual Mars missions, MarsNav could be connected directly to the astronaut's spacesuit to receive readings about remaining oxygen and oxygen consumption.

While spacesuits already provide safety warnings, MarsNav could combine these readings with the astronaut's location and estimated return time. It could recommend returning earlier, skipping scientific stops, or adjusting the mission before oxygen reaches a critical level.

These warnings would work alongside the spacesuit's existing safety systems.

What do we hope to achieve?

Our goal is to develop MarsNav into an exploration companion that helps astronauts conduct meaningful scientific research and make better-informed decisions while exploring Mars.

We are not just building a map of Mars. We are building a tool that helps astronauts decide where to go, what to explore, and how to return home.
